title: The Rain
part: PART FOUR: HOLDING UP THE BRIDGE

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: The River Wend has never flooded Bridgewater, and it never will.*

The rain did not so much fall in Bridgewater as arrive, a thick grey curtain that swallowed the chimneys, the market stalls, and the sound of the world. For three days, the River Wend, usually a placid brown thing that said very little, began to mutter. It was a low, gurgling sound, like a kettle that has forgotten how to whistle but is still trying very hard.

The Kettle & Crumb was full of wet people. Raindrops beaded on the glass front. Inside, the air smelled of damp wool and hot butter. Gran moved behind the counter with the speed of a woman who knows that chaos can be tamed by a second cup.

"The Almanac says it won't flood," said a baker, wringing water from his apron. He looked at Gran with the hopeful, desperate expression of a man who wants the world to be sensible.

Gran did not look up. She was polishing a cup that was already clean. "The Almanac is a book," she said, her voice dry and sharp. "The river is a river. One of them is wet."

Rue stood by the stove, watching the steam rise. Outside, the water was higher than it had been in living memory. It pressed against the shop windows with a quiet, insistent weight.
pages.image: A cozy, crowded tea shop interior with wet townspeople holding cups; Gran, a silver-bunned woman in an apron, polishes a cup at the counter while steam rises from a pot; rain blurs the window glass behind them.

pages.text:
The shop door burst open, letting in a gust of wind and a boy who looked as if he had been rolled in a puddle. Perrin Fen shook his head, sending a small fountain of droplets onto the floorboards. He clutched his notebook to his chest with both hands, protecting the pages with the fierce intensity of a knight guarding a crown jewel.

He was out of breath. His oversized wool hat was askew, and his ink-stained fingers were white-knuckled around the leather cover.

"Rue," he gasped. "The arch."

"Sit down, you'll fall down," Gran said, but she did not move to stop him.

Perrin did not sit. He turned to Rue, his eyes wide and serious. "It has sagged. Another finger-width. Since the day he went in." He swallowed, his throat clicking. "For three weeks, nobody has re-seated the stones. The water is eating the piers. If it goes, it goes at the Fair."

Rue felt a cold knot tighten in her stomach, distinct from the rain. The Fair was tomorrow. The whole town would be on that bridge, the Mayor leading the parade with his top hat and his chain of office.

"He will hold it up," Rue said, though her voice sounded thin in the warm, crowded room.

Perrin looked at her, then at the wet floor. "I hope he is there," he said quietly.
pages.image: A drenched thin boy in an oversized wool hat stands in a tea shop doorway, shaking water, clutching a notebook tightly; Rue, a small freckled girl in a yellow raincoat, listens with a worried expression; Gran watches from the background.

pages.text:
The rain was no longer a curtain but a solid wall, and Rue’s rubber boots splashed through the streets with a sound like small, angry drums. They found the Mayor’s house empty, save for a servant who looked equally soaked and tired. He told them his master was out inspecting the bunting, then shut the door on their question.

"Inspecting?" Rue asked, though her voice was drowned by the drumming rain.

"He believes the green ribbon needs to be taut," the servant said, and did not open the door again.

Next was Skye Tanner, who stood on a crate in the yard, trying to see over the crowd. When Rue explained what Perrin had seen, Skye’s long braid whipped in the wind. She did not sneer, and she did not laugh. She looked at the water, then at Rue, and her face went very still.

"I can get the older children to the Green," Skye said. "But I cannot stop the Mayor. He will be there."

Before Rue could answer, a voice came from the shop window. Gran stood there, her coat buttoned to her chin, her half-moon glasses reflecting the streetlamp.

"I am going to speak to him," she said. "You two stay here. And do not let Biscuit out."
pages.image: Three figures in a rainy street: Rue in a yellow raincoat, Skye in a blue coat, and Gran in a dark coat standing in a shop window; the Mayor’s house is visible in the background with wet bunting; rain streaks the ground.

pages.text:
Gran left with the confidence of a woman who has been arguing with customers for fifty years. Rue and Perrin looked at each other. There was only one place left.

The old bridge was dark. The rain hammered against the stone arches, and the river below was a churning brown mess, inches from the bottom of the arch. The air smelled of wet rock and ancient moss. Rue stopped before the stone door. It was smooth, cold, and utterly silent.

She did not knock. She reached into her pocket and pulled out the button. It was warm in her hand, a small, solid weight. She pressed it gently against the stone, a silent offering.

"I know you don't have to forgive me," Rue said. Her voice was small, but it did not shake. "And I know you don't have to come out. But the bridge is going to fall. And I have never once seen you not hold something up."

The rain fell. The water rushed. She waited.
pages.image: A small girl in a yellow raincoat stands before a massive, smooth stone door under a dark bridge arch; she presses a small wooden button against the stone; rain pours down around her; the river churns violently below the arch.

pages.text:
The silence stretched. It was a heavy, pressing silence, the kind that makes your ears ring and your heart beat too loudly. Rue’s arms ached from holding the button up. The rain soaked through her raincoat, cold and sharp. She wanted to turn and run. She wanted to be anywhere else. But she stayed.

Then, deep inside the stone, there was a sound. It was not a crash. It was a groan, a creak, a low, resonant hum that vibrated through the soles of her boots. It sounded like an enormous door remembering how to move, like a mountain stretching after a long sleep.

A thin line of gold light appeared at the edge of the stones. It was the lantern. The lantern she had mended. It flickered once, twice, and then held steady, casting a warm, small glow in the dark, wet world.
pages.image: A thin line of golden light glows from the crack of a massive stone door in a dark, rainy bridge arch; the light is steady and warm; the girl in the yellow raincoat watches with hope; rain falls around the light.
